29.other: how everyday objects from long ago can still interest young people today
29.reason: Gist item: the passage shows an old object (the iron) drawing questions from younger students who tried to lift it, and the old music box also got smiles, so this broader theme is a partly right summary a careful student could defend. The key is more specific (the writer's view that the iron was dull, then interest), but the rival is supported by the passage rather than merely far off. Borderline; flagged under the asymmetric-cost rule.

31.note: Key text says the object 'seemed boring to her', but the first-person writer's gender is never established in the passage (the only 'her' references are the grandmother). Not release-blocking for a reading item, but worth fixing to 'to the writer'.

batch_patterns.evidence: Every multi-sentence main-idea item uses the same option cast: one single-paragraph detail, one contradicted/reversed claim, one over-general 'how X in general' line (5C clubs earn money, 16C good roads, 23C new technology, 29A everyday objects, 33D team members, 38D many kinds of fish, 44B places for families) and the key. The general option is never the key in 7/7, so a student can eliminate it plus the detail by shape alone, leaving key vs one contradicted option. Weak tell (it is a common test convention), not item-level. Checked and clean: key letters B15 D13 C11 A9 with no ABCD run; key uniquely longest in only 8/48.
